#9740. iOS Startup Performance in Practice, Part 2: Measuring App Launch Time in Production

How to measure startup on real user devices, define trustworthy production percentiles, and use XCTest and Instruments to explain regressions.

The easiest way to measure app launch time is to start a stopwatch, open the app, and write down the number.

It is also one of the easiest ways to produce a measurement that cannot be reproduced, compared, or trusted.

An iOS launch depends on more than the code in the repository. The result changes with the process state, system caches, device model, thermal state, available memory, network behavior, stored user data, app version, and the destination the user is trying to open. Two measurements can both be technically correct while describing different experiences.

In Part 1, we separated cold launch, warm launch, resume, scene creation, and entry points. We also defined three possible endpoints: First Draw, Meaningful Content, and Time to Interactive.

Now we can turn that model into a measurement system.

This article is the second part of iOS Startup Performance in Practice, a six-part series:

The goal of this part is not to find a single perfect number. It is to build a production measurement system that describes what real users experience - and then use controlled tests and profiling to explain why that distribution changes.

Suppose one engineer reports a launch time of 1.4 seconds and another reports 2.1 seconds. Before comparing them, we need to know:

Without these answers, the numbers are labels rather than evidence.

Let’s start with production metrics. For every launch metric, define a measurement contract:

Real user launches of app version `8.24.0`

New-process launch; resume reported separately

Icon, link, notification, and quick action segmented where custom telemetry allows it

System launch start for MetricKit; first application marker for custom metrics

First Draw for the system metric; Home Interactive for the product metric

Signed-out and authenticated users reported separately

Device performance tier, iOS version, app version, and migration state

Seven complete days after the target rollout reaches a stable cohort

MetricKit or Organizer for system launch; custom telemetry for product milestones

Internal builds, synthetic runs, invalid or incomplete milestone sequences

This table describes measurement on user devices. There are no fixed test phones, stubbed networks, or XCTest iterations in the production contract. Real device and network diversity are not noise to remove; they are part of the experience we are trying to understand.

The first rule of launch measurement is therefore:

Define the population and user-visible endpoint before naming the number.

Instead of writing “launch time is 1.8 seconds,” write:

For production new-process launches of version 8.24.x, Time to First Draw is 1.1 seconds at p50 and 1.8 seconds at p90 across 2.4 million samples. Authenticated users on the lowest device tier have a p90 of 2.6 seconds.

The values are illustrative, but the form is important: it tells us who experienced the delay, which boundary was measured, and whether the percentile is statistically meaningful.

There is a fundamental limitation in iOS startup measurement:

This means one production number cannot answer every startup question.

Use Xcode Organizer or MetricKit to understand the system-observed launch distribution. These sources can describe Time to First Draw, optimized launch behavior influenced by prewarming, resume duration, and extended launch measurements supported by the OS version.

This is the authoritative source for questions such as:

Use lightweight custom telemetry for milestones the operating system cannot infer:

This is the authoritative source for questions such as:

Do not present an application timer that begins in didFinishLaunching as full launch time. Name it by its actual boundaries, for example AppCodeToHomeInteractive or RouteReceivedToDestinationInteractive.

Together, the two clocks give us a useful production model:

System launch distribution and device/OS trends

Entry-point-specific Meaningful Content and TTI

Instruments, XCTest, Xcode Organizer, MetricKit, and custom telemetry do not compete with one another. They answer different questions.

What startup time do real users experience?

Organizer, MetricKit, and production milestone telemetry

How does the distribution change by app version, device, OS, or user state?

Production telemetry segmented by those dimensions

How long until a requested destination becomes useful?

Which application service delays startup?

Separate resume metric and lifecycle instrumentation

A common mistake is to use the most convenient tool and then reformulate the problem so that it aligns with the result obtained using that tool.

How long does this scenario take under defined conditions?

These activities form a loop, but they should not be confused:

Instruments collects thread states, samples, stack traces, allocations, signposts, and launch phases. That visibility has a cost. Apple explicitly demonstrates that CPU time and wall-clock time in an instrumented trace can differ because profiling itself introduces overhead. It makes Instruments a diagnostic tool rather than the final stopwatch.

Use production data to discover and quantify the problem. Use Instruments to explain its root causes. Use XCTest to make the reproduction scenario repeatable and protect the issue from returning. Then, refer back to production data to verify the result.

As soon as production data reveals which cohort or user journey is performing slowly, create a benchmark that reproduces the situation. This serves as a tool for diagnosing and preventing regressions, rather than as a primary description of the user experience.

Launch tests are sensitive to the state of the whole device. A useful benchmark removes unrelated variance while preserving the characteristic that made the production cohort slow: device class, data volume, migration state, authentication path, or entry point.

The simulator is useful for development, lifecycle experiments, and fast feedback. It is not a reliable representation of iPhone launch performance because it runs on Mac hardware, shares host resources, and does not reproduce the same storage, memory, thermal, scheduling, and rendering environment.

Use physical devices for performance conclusions.

The minimum useful device set normally includes:

Do not compare an “after” result from a new phone with a “before” result from an old one.

Measure a Release configuration, or a dedicated Performance configuration derived from Release.

Avoid drawing conclusions from a Debug build. Debugger attachment, assertions, sanitizers, logging, and the absence of compiler optimizations can change both the duration and the shape of launch.

Keep observability enabled, but make it lightweight. Signposts are designed for this purpose; verbose synchronous logging is not.

Do not cool the device only for the “after” measurement. The goal is not to produce the smallest possible number. The goal is to make before and after comparable.

Startup often depends more on user state than teams initially expect.

The fixture should be deterministic. A performance test that uses an account whose data changes every day is not deterministic even if the test code never changes.

The network is part of the user experience, but it is usually a poor dependency for a code-regression benchmark. Latency, DNS, TLS, server load, routing, and radio state can overwhelm a small application-side change.

For local and CI measurements, prefer one of these contracts:

Then validate real network behavior separately in production.

There is no public API that reliably clears every relevant system cache and requests a “true cold launch.” Force-quitting an app and immediately reopening it creates a new process, but the second launch can still benefit from warmed pages and system services.

Apple recommends warm launches for repeatable development measurements because they are more consistent. XCTest also performs a throwaway iteration before recording measured iterations, reducing first-run cache variance.

That does not mean cold launch is unimportant. It means it needs a different strategy.

Use warm launches for high-signal regression detection:

Evaluate cold behavior through a combination of:

Never label “terminate and immediately relaunch five times” as five cold launches. It is five new-process launches under increasingly warm system conditions.

XCTApplicationLaunchMetric provides the most practical automated baseline for application launch.

A minimal UI performance test looks like this:

Without an extended launch task, XCTApplicationLaunchMetric() measures to the first frame. XCTest runs the measured block repeatedly and ignores an additional initial iteration used to reduce warm-up variance.

If the requirement is that the first frame is also responsive to input, use:

This waits until the main thread is responsive after the first frame. It is often a better default for products that can technically draw a frame while still blocking user interaction.

The two metrics answer different questions:

First frame, plus any explicitly registered extended launch tasks

XCTApplicationLaunchMetric(waitUntilResponsive: true)

Do not silently switch between them when comparing builds.

Launch arguments and environment variables are useful for choosing deterministic fixtures, but the application must process them carefully.

Do not replace the normal startup architecture with a completely different test-only app. The test should control external variance, not remove the code you intend to measure.

A production application usually needs several launch tests:

Entry-point-specific journeys can be added separately, but remember that the built-in application launch metric ends at a system launch milestone. If the product destination becomes useful later, add an application-owned measurement for that interval.

Xcode performance tests can compare results with an accepted baseline and flag regressions. A baseline is only meaningful for a stable environment.

Do not share one absolute baseline across:

For CI, record the device identity, OS, Xcode version, commit, build configuration, fixture, and raw measurements with every run. If any of those dimensions changes, treat the comparison as a new series until you have evidence that the values remain comparable.

Once the benchmark shows that launch is slow, open the same scenario with the App Launch template in Instruments.

Profile a Release build on the same class of physical device used for measurement.

The App Launch template separates major phases such as:

In the trace, inspect more than the total duration:

Pin the app launch phases, main thread, and relevant worker threads. Add Points of Interest so that application-owned phases appear on the same timeline.

Then form one narrow hypothesis. For example:

The root interface waits synchronously for the complete catalog cache, although the first screen needs only the first page.

Change that behavior, return to the controlled XCTest, and measure again. Do not report the duration of the new Instruments trace as the improvement; report the repeated benchmark under the original contract.

System metrics can tell us when the first frame appears. They cannot infer that a product screen contains meaningful data or that a requested route is ready.

Use OSSignposter to make application phases visible:

A small interval wrapper can keep ownership explicit:

The end marker must represent a real product condition. For a home screen, that may require:

Do not end the interval because a convenient callback fired.

XCTest can record the duration between matching signpost events:

This creates an application-specific benchmark, but it has an important boundary: the signpost cannot begin before application code runs. It measures the application-owned interval, not the full system launch.

Good startup signposts are few, stable, and architectural:

Avoid adding an interval around every function. A trace with hundreds of unstable names becomes harder to compare and expensive to maintain.

Signpost names also become part of the observability contract. Rename them deliberately.

An app can produce a fast first frame and still feel slow.

The system First Draw metric may report approximately one second. The user asked for a product and could not act on it for three and a half seconds.

The problem begins when the first number is presented as the complete user experience.

Define a product milestone for each important entry point:

Requested product visible and primary action enabled

Camera preview active and accepting input

This is also why a universal “startup budget” is insufficient. The system launch budget can be shared, but route execution and destination readiness need their own budgets.

Production launch performance is a distribution across users, devices, operating systems, application states, and entry points. A single average hides the experiences that most need attention.

For production launch data, report at least:

Always segment the distribution before interpreting it. At minimum, compare:

A global p90 can remain unchanged while the p90 on the oldest supported devices regresses by several seconds. It can also appear to improve simply because adoption shifted toward newer devices. Segmentation is part of the metric, not an optional dashboard filter.

Do not use production maximum as a release KPI. In a sufficiently large population, isolated extreme values are expected and may reflect interruptions the application cannot control. Use high percentiles, SLO compliance, and sample count to quantify the tail; use diagnostics to investigate pathological individual cases.

For a controlled test, preserve every raw iteration and report the median, p90, and maximum. A small local dataset answers a different question: whether the scenario is stable enough to reproduce a change.

Suppose ten controlled runs produce these durations in seconds:

The median describes the center, while the p90 and maximum reveal instability that an average would blur. Do not delete the slow runs merely because they are inconvenient. Investigate whether they came from the application or from a documented failure of the experiment.

Ten local runs can provide quick feedback, but they do not make a production-quality p99. High percentiles require many samples.

Do not compare a p90 from ten local launches with a p90 from millions of production launches as though they were the same experiment.

Production data is the primary description of startup quality. Controlled tests answer whether a code change affected a reproducible scenario, but they cannot represent every real user.

Xcode Organizer aggregates launch performance from users who share diagnostics and allows teams to compare distributions across app versions and devices. It is the fastest way to establish a system-level production baseline before building any custom pipeline.

MetricKit reports include histogrammed launch and resume information rather than one application-wide scalar. Depending on the OS and SDK generation, launch data includes time-to-first-draw, optimized time-to-first-draw for prewarmed launches, resume time, and extended launch measurements.

Apple is evolving MetricKit toward the newer MetricManager, MetricReport, and typed MetricResult APIs in upcoming SDKs. If you adopt those APIs, isolate the SDK-specific ingestion layer. The measurement model should remain stable even when the transport type changes:

Do not upload a daily payload and discard its dimensions. At minimum, preserve:

Aggregating everything into one average makes regressions on older devices almost invisible.

System metrics understand launch and rendering. They do not automatically know that the product card requested by a notification is ready for purchase.

Avoid including raw URLs, notification payloads, user identifiers, search text, or product data unless the analytics design explicitly requires and permits them. The useful dimensions are normally categories, not content.

Startup observability runs on the critical path, so its design matters.

A lightweight custom recorder might look like this:

Even this code starts only after application code exists. It must never be described as measuring the full interval from the user tap.

The following protocol is a useful starting point for a production team. It begins with user devices and introduces laboratory measurements only after the production metric identifies a problem.

Select the launch scenarios that represent meaningful user traffic and risk:

Keep launch and resume in separate series.

Before creating test fixtures, define the production segments needed to explain the journey: app version, device tier, OS, authentication state, entry-point category, and migration state. Do not collect dimensions that have no analytical purpose.

Use Organizer or MetricKit for system launch and resume distributions. Add lightweight custom milestones for Meaningful Content and Time to Interactive. Buffer and upload the data outside the launch critical path.

Collect a complete, stable rollout window. Report p50, p90, p95, sample count, SLO compliance, and the important segments. Treat resume as a separate metric.

Determine whether the regression belongs to a device tier, OS, app version, entry point, user state, or migration path. This cohort becomes the specification for the controlled experiment.

Choose stable physical devices based on the affected production population. Create deterministic fixtures that reproduce its data volume, authentication state, feature flags, cache state, and network contract.

Use XCTApplicationLaunchMetric for First Draw or responsiveness and signposts for application-owned stages. Use Instruments to connect the slow interval to threads, stacks, dependencies, and launch phases.

Measure after every meaningful change. Once the improvement is reproducible, run the benchmark regularly on fixed hardware and alert on a sustained regression or budget violation rather than one noisy sample.

Compare Organizer, MetricKit, and custom product milestones by app version and the original affected segment. A local win is complete only when the relevant production distribution moves in the expected direction.

A production report should first show the user impact and the affected cohort, then connect it to the controlled experiment used to explain the change:

The exact values above are illustrative. The important property is traceability: the report begins with the real-user regression, identifies the cohort, shows how it was reproduced, and defines how the fix will be validated.

Faster for which scenario, device, endpoint, and percentile?

At this point, the pieces form one system:

Each layer corrects a blind spot in another:

The goal is not to choose one source of truth. It is to know which source is authoritative for each question.

Correct launch measurement begins with real users.

First define the production population, lifecycle path, entry point, start boundary, and meaningful endpoint. Collect enough samples to report p50, p90, p95, SLO compliance, and the device, OS, app-version, and user-state segments that can explain the distribution.

A benchmark tells you whether the code changed. Production telemetry tells you whether the user experience changed.

In Part 3: Finding Bottlenecks from dyld to the First Frame, we will use the measurement system built here to read an App Launch trace phase by phase. We will examine pre-main work, linked frameworks, static initialization, disk I/O, main-thread blocking, rendering, and the difference between CPU time and waiting time.

#9738. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

Try it on your own documents here. To learn more about Dharma-AI and the specialized models we build, visit dharma-ai.com.

Explore Dharma AI on Hugging Face to try our interactive demos, download our open-source models, and discover how specialized AI systems outperform general-purpose models in real enterprise applications.

#9737. How to prebake pie crust — and why you should: The key to flaky — not flabby — pie crust.

A soggy bottom. Not something you want for your baby. Or your pie crust. And while we can’t help you with your baby, there’s a simple solution to pies with soggy bottoms: prebake (also known as blind bake) the crust.

There are a number of reasons your pie can end up with a soft, pale, underbaked crust — and steps you can take to help prevent that unfortunate result.

But the one surefire way to make certain your pie’s crust will be golden brown, crisp, and delicious — just as appealing as its filling — is to prebake it. That’s right: bake the bottom crust first, before adding the filling.

Most commonly, it's smart to prebake pie crust when:

But some fillings might instead cook fully on the stovetop, like the rich, thick filling for chocolate cream pie. When it’s done, you simply pour it into its crust — and said crust had better be prebaked to perfection, since the pie’s not going anywhere near an oven.

Other pies, typically those with a more delicate, egg- and cream-based filling (think custard pie or quiche) require at least some baking — but don’t spend long enough in the oven (at a high enough temperature) to guarantee a fully baked, brown and crispy crust.

In these cases, you need to prebake your crust.

The recipe you're following may explain explicitly how to prebake your crust. But if it doesn't, follow this process:

First, roll your bottom crust and place it in the pan. Crimp or flatten the edge. Chill it for 30 minutes, to relax the gluten and firm up the fat(s); this will help prevent shrinkage, so don't skip!

Line the crust with foil, parchment, or a paper coffee filter. Fill it about two-thirds full with dried beans, uncooked rice (or other uncooked grain berries), pie weights, or granulated sugar.

Bake the crust in a preheated 375°F oven for 20 minutes, set on a baking stone or steel if you have one. Remove the crust from the oven and lift out the liner and weights. (If you’ve used sugar, save it for your future baking; it’ll be lightly toasted and yummy!)

At this point your crust is partially prebaked, and good for any of your pies that tend to exhibit a wan, flabby bottom crust when done. Think pumpkin pie: You don’t want to bake the filling so long that it’s stiff and dry, but you may pull your pie out of the oven to find your perfectly baked filling is resting in a partially baked crust. Prebaking your crust partway is a sensible solution for this scenario.

To fully prebake the crust, prick the bottom all over with a fork to prevent bubbles. Return the crust to the oven and bake for an additional 20 to 25 minutes, until it’s golden all over.

If, despite your best efforts, the lined, weighted crust still slips down the inside of the pan while it prebakes, try this: Bake the crust upside down.

To start, you’ll need two identical (or nicely nestable) pie pans with flat rims.

Place your rolled-out crust in one of the pans, anchoring it to the rim of the pan with a fork-tine crimp. Place a liner of some kind (same as above: parchment, foil, coffee filter) into the pan. Nest the second pan into the first.

Pick up both pans, turn them over, and set them on a baking sheet. Place the baking sheet and pie pans in the oven, and bake as directed above. As the crust bakes, gravity will pull it down toward its rim — rather than into a puddle at the bottom of the pan. Magic!

After 20 minutes remove the baking sheet from the oven, carefully turn the pans over, lift out the empty pan, and remove the liner. At this point, your crust is partially prebaked. To prebake it fully, place the crust back in the oven, right side up, and bake until it's golden.

If you struggle with a pale, pasty bottom crust in your fruit pie, then yes, you can prebake it — with a couple of caveats:

So, soggy bottoms begone! From now on I expect every pie you bake will have a deep golden brown, flaky, crispy crust on the bottom — all because of the prebake.

And if you have any other questions about pie — from creating tender, flaky crust to thickening fruit filling to assessing when your pie is perfectly baked — please check out our Pie Baking Guide.

#9736. A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.

Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you.

We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard.

Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate.

Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both.

We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design.

Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages.

Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio. Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes.

It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now. Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license.

The launch came with demos from friends and from our own team. On an Apple Watch with Wi-Fi off, Phonon talks you through a coffee brew step by step. On an iPhone with no signal, it counts your reps and keeps you going. A robot called Lamp, from Autonomous, wears a sorting hat and talks in character. In a browser, an offline dino runner becomes a radio show hosted by Rex. There's also a sci-fi game voiced on the player's own machine, and Proust read aloud page by page.

The Hugging Face team built the Transformers integration, so developers could use Phonon in Transformers from day one.

Developers have started building on it too. An ExecuTorch conversion runs Phonon on a visitor's GPU in the browser, Micdrop brings it to Node.js apps, and Spaces like smallest-s2s build on it.

Phonon was downloaded more than 200,000 times in its first two weeks, and it’s still trending on Hugging Face.

The Open TTS Leaderboard is a very new project from Hugging Face, and we love it. With more than 9,000 TTS models on the Hugging Face Hub, the leaderboard gives developers one place to compare open models and hear them side by side. Across 23 languages, models are evaluated on intelligibility (word error rate of the outputs), speed (inverse real-time factor and time-to-first audio), and naturalness (UTMOS for English and KOMOS for Korean). Fixed-voice and voice cloning are evaluated, with an additional speaker similarity metric for the latter. The leaderboard also has a Listen tab, where you can conveniently compare TTS outputs yourself and vote for the ones you like the most.

On intelligibility, Phonon ranks first in German and Spanish, and in the top three in every language we evaluated, next to models up to 100 times its size.

Speed is where we see Phonon truly shine, as the models top the CPU streaming benchmark on time-to-first audio.

We built a new inference framework, ptts, specifically for Phonon. The goal of ptts is to get the best performance on a wide variety of devices and as such supports more than 10 backends: CPU (Intel, Arm, WebAssembly), GPU (CUDA, Vulkan, Metal, WebGPU), and NPU (Apple Core ML, Snapdragon®).

Phonon is also available in 🤗 Transformers, from v5.21, as its reference PyTorch implementation. Where ptts runs a single stream on device, Transformers targets GPU throughput: batched generation, full-graph torch.compile, e.g., for synthesizing speech datasets at scale. Being native PyTorch, it is a base to build upon, whether to integrate Phonon into your own stack or to study the model itself.

It belongs to the Pocket TTS lineage, so we first added Pocket TTS to Transformers. Phonon sits on top as a modular model: about 200 lines describing only what differs.

Phonon generates audio latents autoregressively: each step outputs a latent that is fed back as the next input, and the training loss is computed on them. Latents are the model's inputs, outputs and targets, as text tokens are for a language model, so the codec mapping audio to latents plays the role of a tokenizer. Transformers ships it as such: an audio tokenizer, held by the processor next to the text tokenizer:

A voice is not a recording but a tensor of speaker latents. Phonon never encodes audio directly with its audio tokenizer, which ships decoder-only, and voices come precomputed: gradium/phonon-voices.

The prompt layout (voice positions, text, then a token opening the audio) ships with the checkpoint as a chat template, as for other multimodal models in Transformers. You write a standard conversation, with an empty audio item where the voice goes, and your code stays the same across checkpoints. The processor then expands the voice placeholder to one position per frame, normalizes and tokenizes the text, and batches the inputs:

generate returns latents, which the processor decodes to audio:

Phonon can speak with any voice. Clone one from a short recording with the speaker’s consent, or describe a new one in plain text in Gradium Studio. Then download the voice file, load it in Phonon, and it runs fully on the device.

We also train custom Phonon models with design partners. If your memory budget is tight, we can make the model smaller. If you need Korean, Arabic or Japanese, we can train for that too. And if your product has its own vocabulary, we can fine-tune on it. Get in touch and tell us what you need.

Thank you to the Hugging Face team, and to everyone who tried Phonon in its first two weeks.

Phonon is our first open release. Try it out and tell us what you build.

#9735. 2 Supplements That Significantly Reduce Heart Disease And Cancer Risk

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

The most recent trial confirms that two nutrients can reduce deaths from heart attacks and cancer.

Omega-3 fatty acids from fish oil can significantly reduce heart attacks and vitamin D supplementation can significantly lower the number of deaths caused by different types of cancer.

Researchers studied 26,000 American adults in the VITAL clinical trial for five years to see if fish oil or vitamin D would definitely ward off cardiovascular disease or cancer.

The outcomes were reassuring: marine omega-3 fatty acid intake was linked to a significant drop in heart attacks.

One-and-half servings per week of dietary fish intake showed the maximum heart health benefits, but higher dietary fish intake didn’t help more.

The greatest decrease in heart attacks was seen in African-Americans.

The benefit of 1 gram of omega-3 fish oil supplementation showed a small decrease in major cardiovascular events like stroke and death from cardiovascular disease.

Vitamin D3 or cholecalciferol intake at a dose of 2000 IU per day showed a significant decrease of death from cancer for those who took it for at least two years.

However, supplementation with vitamin D3 capsules didn’t significantly lower incidence of any type of cancer or cardiovascular disease.

Dr. JoAnn Manson, the study’s first author, said:

“The pattern of findings suggests a complex balance of benefits and risks for each intervention and points to the need for additional research to determine which individuals may be most likely to derive a net benefit from these supplements.”

Dr. Stephanie Faubion, NAMS medical director, said:

“With heart disease and cancer representing the most significant health threats to women, it is imperative that we continue to study the viability of options that prevent these diseases and help women survive them.”

The 1 gram omega-3 fish oil supplementation used in the VITAL clinical trial was Omacor, a prescription medicine for adults.

The capsule contains 840 milligrams marine omega-3 fatty acids, of which 465 mg is eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and 375 mg is docosahexaenoic acid (DHA).

The study was presented at the North American Menopause Society (NAMS) Annual Meeting in Chicago (Manson et al., 2019).

#9734. New NVIDIA Cosmos 3 Open Models for Interactive World Simulation

NVIDIA Cosmos world model development platform adds four new open-weight checkpoints to its Cosmos 3 model family for generating interactive world simulation and multi-sensor multi-view driving scenes:

All four models are post-trained examples of Cosmos 3 Nano and have 16B trainable parameters. The models use OpenMDW1.1, permitting commercial and non-commercial use under its terms.

Download the checkpoints · Read the technical report . Watch the demos

🦾 Robotics needs environments that can answer this across changing scenes and viewpoints. These checkpoints offer complementary ways to build them: Sim-Bimanual predicts visual consequences from actions, while Sim-Transfer turns a physics simulator’s controls into generated observations.

🚦 For autonomous driving, appearance and geometry must agree. Synchronized camera and LiDAR generation connects visual observations with 3D sensing. Scene and traffic-signal controls let researchers vary road layouts and signal states, then study how a driving policy responds.

🔄 Each observation can shape the next action. Streaming generation connects video prediction to ongoing interaction, giving world-model researchers a way to explore how actions and observations unfold together.

🌐 An open foundation for others to build on. NVIDIA’s vision is to help researchers and developers create richer, more responsive simulated worlds. Open weights and post-training recipes provide a shared starting point for adapting models, comparing methods, and contributing improvements. These problems remain hard: the work ahead is to measure where the models faithfully support policy learning and evaluation, understand their limits, and improve where they fall short.

Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto is a bidirectional model for offline synthetic driving data generation. It generates synchronized video across up to 11 camera views, including fisheyes, and supports joint RGB–LiDAR generation. Per-camera World Scenario Map (WSM) controls specify scene structure and traffic motion, while text prompts guide appearance.

Developers can vary environmental conditions to expand training and evaluation coverage, with optional initial RGB images to anchor scene appearance. Joint LiDAR generation additionally uses aligned HD-map range-map controls. Transfer-Auto also serves as the foundation for adapting Cosmos to your own sensor rig and driving domain. Start by post-training it on your data to accommodate your camera layout, LiDAR configuration, and target environment. The adapted model can be used directly for offline data generation or undergo causal training and few-step distillation for fast streaming simulation—the development path used to create Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Transfer-Auto

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto is the causally distilled streaming variant of Transfer-Auto. It generates successive small chunks of synchronized camera video and LiDAR in just a few denoising steps, using generated history and updated driving controls to support fast streaming and long, interactive rollouts.

Provide per-camera captions and synchronized WSM controls, optionally adding initial RGB images. For LiDAR generation, include HD-Map range controls aligned with the camera controls. The distilled model generates successive chunks using its rolling history. Closed-loop interaction requires a simulation runtime and WSM renderer to update those controls from driving inputs. For a new sensor rig or domain, adapt Transfer-Auto first, then distill it into Sim-Auto.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Auto

Your simulator computes motion, contacts, and physical state. Sim-Transfer uses its spatial controls and a text prompt to render color observations that a policy can consume.

Action → simulator update → spatial controls → generated RGB → next policy action

Depth: relative distance from the camera.

Segmentation: regions and object boundaries.

Text guides appearance; physics and ground-truth state stay with the simulator.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Transfer

Output Video From Sim-Bimanual Simulation Checkpoint

Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual simulates how an environment evolves in response to a bimanual robot’s actions. It supports interactive two-arm simulation for YAM and AgiBot embodiments, controlled by a policy or human-operated joysticks.

Start with an image, move the robot or camera, and generate the next observations. One control sequence can switch between viewpoint changes and manipulation.

The mixed-action example uses 59 control values, padded to 64 during training. Its schema defines coordinate frames, rotations, gripper calibration, validity masks, and control domains. Follow those conventions so each value describes the intended motion.

Keep timing aligned: T transitions need T+1 observations. Training transforms raw captures into the model’s action representation; released inference actions are already normalized.

Here, Sim-Transfer generates visuals from a physics simulator’s updated state; Sim-Bimanual generates the next observation directly from the scene and robot actions.

Requirements: Linux, an NVIDIA GPU, Docker, and NVIDIA Container Toolkit. The published vLLM-Omni setup was tested on one GB200; this is not a minimum-memory specification. The server downloads weights; the clients fetch sample inputs.

Point your agent to the open skill : Run inference with Cosmos3-Nano-Sim-Bimanual

Cosmos 3’s Mixture-of-Transformers backbone connects separate text-processing and visual-generation networks through attention. The generator predicts each short segment from the prompt, available controls, and generated history.

Controls + history → generate chunk → decode images → update history

Denoising refines noisy, compressed video representations into a segment. Temporal-causal attention lets it read available history and controls while blocking future target observations. A key/value cache retains attention information for the next prediction.

The model operates on compressed video representations called latents. After the initial image, each latent time step represents four RGB frames. Transfer predicts one step per chunk; the optimized Bimanual setup in the report predicts two. Smaller chunks let new controls affect generation more often.

Stage 0 — Bidirectional adaptation: learn the domain and its control-to-video relationships from complete recorded clips.

Stage 1 — Teacher forcing: predict each chunk from earlier recorded observations and available controls, with the clean answer and future targets masked out.

Stage 2 — Consistency distillation: use a frozen teacher to train a student that generates each chunk in four denoising steps.

Stage 3 — Self-forcing: train on the student’s generated history. A frozen teacher and an auxiliary score model supply the distribution-matching signal.

Why the final stage matters: a slightly mispredicted object becomes context for later frames, so errors can compound. Self-forcing exposes training to that generated history. Distillation and caching reduce the cost of producing each observation.

The post-training recipes start from Cosmos3-Nano or compatible base weights and cover all four stages. Keep full training checkpoints to resume; exported inference weights omit optimizer and other training state.

Transfer-auto: Post-train on your driving data to adapt to your sensor rig and domain, and generate offline synthetic data.

Sim-auto: Apply causal training and distillation to an adapted Transfer-Auto model for fast streaming simulation.

Sim-Transfer : Post-train the checkpoint for your environment with local data preparation, stage configurations, and resume.

Sim-Bimanual: Post-train for your embodiment with data validation, stage configurations, checkpoint handoffs, and export.

Give your coding agent the skill and dataset location. Follow the environment checks, validate a sample, and test training and restart before a longer run. Evaluate quality on held-out episodes: a successful short run verifies execution, not convergence.

#9733. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. #9731. This Vitamin Reduces Mental Health Problems By 50%

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of this vitamin.

A triple dose of vitamin D3 supplementation in the first two years of life reduces the chance of mental health problems later on by around 50 percent, a high-quality experiment finds.

Infants who were given 30 µg of vitamin D daily, which is three times the recommended dose, were only half as likely to have internalising problems by age 6-8.

Internalising problems are those in which a person keeps their problems to themselves, including depression, anxiety, loneliness and withdrawal.

Dr Samuel Sandboge, the study’s first author, said:

“Our results suggest that a higher dose of vitamin D3 supplementation during the first years of life may reduce the risk of internalizing psychiatric symptoms in late preschool and early school age.”

The randomised controlled trial, which was carried out in Finland, was inspired by the link found between low childhood vitamin D levels and mental health problems.

Almost 350 children were given either a dose of 10 µg or 30 µg of vitamin D from age 2 weeks until 2-years-old.

The results showed that at 6- to 8-years-old, almost 12 percent of children given 10 µg had significant internalising problems.

In the 30 µg group, though, this figure was under 6 percent.

No differences were seen in the number of externalising problems.

Externalising disorders include ADHD and conduct disorder.

Later in life externalising disorders include substance abuse, antisocial personality disorders and even psychopathy.

Dr Samuel Sandboge warned that the study has drawbacks:

“The results and their potential implications are interesting, but further research is needed to confirm the results.

In the interpretation of the results, we must note, among other things, that we studied the psychiatric symptoms only as parent-reported.

Furthermore, the participants of the study were children with Nordic ancestry living in Finland who had good levels of vitamin D.”

Around half the world’s population are thought to have an insufficiency of vitamin D, and 10 percent are deficient.

Vitamin D plays an important role in the development of the brain.

It is notable that a rise in autism and ADHD rates has happened at a time when there have been significant drops in average levels of vitamin D.

The study was published in JAMA Network Open (Sandboge et al., 2023).
